title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Resolve two quotient bits per step in the combinational divider
motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns worst path runs from the MEM/WB destination
register through forwarding and the EX ALU. The ALU evaluates signed and
unsigned division and remainder combinationally. A chain of quotient-bit
decisions is a plausible source of the reported 156-cell path. Shortening
it would raise the clock rate for every CoreMark instruction.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Implement DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU with one unrolled radix-4 restoring
divider inside the ALU. Each of 16 steps consumes two dividend bits and
computes three trial differences in parallel. Their borrow flags select
both the next quotient digit and an already computed remainder. This
halves the number of serial digit decisions relative to binary restoring
division. The ALU still returns its result in EX, so the prediction is
the same 4,491,485 marker-bracketed cycles at a higher median Gowin Fmax.
The main timing risk is the routing and selection delay of the three
parallel differences per step.

changes.description:
In the real DIV/REM datapath, form unsigned operand magnitudes and
precompute D, 2D and 3D once at 34-bit precision. Start with remainder
zero. At step k (1 through 16), append the next two most-significant
unconsumed dividend bits to the remainder. This trial dividend fits
in 2k bits. For each divisor multiple, subtract its low 2k bits with
an explicit borrow output. A trial fits when its upper multiple bits
are zero and the subtraction has no borrow. Select the largest fitting
multiple (or zero), emit its two-bit index and pass the corresponding
difference (or the trial dividend) to the next step. Decode the fit
flags into mutually exclusive selects so the three trials stay parallel.
Select quotient or remainder, then apply the quotient's XOR sign or
the dividend's sign for remainder. Handle a zero divisor explicitly
with all ones for DIV/DIVU and the original dividend for REM/REMU.
Use 32-bit magnitude and sign correction so INT_MIN / -1 returns
INT_MIN with zero remainder. Preserve the existing ALTOPS formulas.

Exercise quotient-digit transitions with dividends one below, at and

divisors with 2D or 3D above 32 bits, mixed signed operands, and
quotients with alternating base-4 digits. Check both quotient and
remainder against an integer reference that truncates toward zero.

title: Move DIV and REM off the single-cycle execute path
motivation:
The baseline scores 12.12 iterations/s at 5.442 MHz. Gowin reports a 199.837 ns path through operand forwarding and the EX ALU with 156 cells. The ALU computes signed and unsigned quotient and remainder combinationally. Full-width division is the strongest candidate for that depth.

Disassembly of the canonical RV32IM -O3 CoreMark binary shows exactly five DIVU instructions, all in main. The measured start_time, iterate and stop_time calls are at 0x1220, 0x1228 and 0x122c. Neither iterate nor any of its callees contains a DIV or REM instruction. Moving division across clock edges therefore carries no direct latency cost in the measured loop.

Give DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU one shared, blocking restoring divider in EX. Capture the forwarded operands and sign flags at issue. Run four registered rounds of eight binary quotient steps each on unsigned magnitudes. Each step uses the borrow from a trial subtraction to choose the next remainder and quotient bit. A separate completion cycle selects quotient or remainder and applies the RV32M sign and exceptional-case rules. The start, four rounds and completion take six EX cycles, which leaves room for a load-use or redirect bubble within the formal progress window.

Hold fetch and ID/EX while the divide is pending. Drain older instructions and inject side-effect-free EX/MEM bubbles until the result can advance. Issue once, only when an older memory request can advance, and capture both original source values for RVFI before the forwarding sources drain. Transfer the result once through the ordinary EX/MEM forwarding and retirement path. Integer ALU operations and all multiplies retain their single-cycle EX latency.

A 50% gain at the baseline's 4,491,485 bracketed cycles would require 8.16 MHz. The prediction is that cutting the division recurrence from 32 steps to eight per clock will clear that frequency with little change in bracketed cycles. Compare median Gowin Fmax and marker-to-marker cycles separately to test that prediction.

title: Predict direct branches at fetch with a 128-entry bimodal table
motivation:
IF and ID share a cycle in this core. Fetch always selects PC+4, so a taken
transfer resolved in EX discards one fetch slot. Between the MMIO markers,
294,425 conditional branches select a nonsequential PC and 49,367 JALs
execute. With both bus stalls enabled, the 128-entry prototype completed
ten CoreMark iterations in 4,202,272 bracketed cycles and matched all five
canonical CRCs. This saves 289,213 cycles and raises iterations/cycle by 6.88%.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use the fetched instruction to identify legal conditional branches and JAL.
In parallel with immediate generation, read a 128-entry table of two-bit
saturating counters indexed by the fetch PC. For a conditional branch use

target on a taken prediction and PC+4 otherwise. JALR resolves in EX.
Computing direct targets from the current instruction makes table aliasing
affect only direction and requires just one prediction bit per instruction.

After initialization, train once per valid conditional branch advancing
from EX. A correct prediction lets an accepted fetch enter ID/EX on the
resolution edge.
A mismatch flushes that fetch and loads the architectural successor into
the PC. The prototype's three Gowin placement options reached 5.155,
5.488 and 5.488 MHz. Combining the median with the measured cycle count
yields 13.06 iter/s, 7.75% above the 12.12 baseline. Placement option 0
used 533 additional logic cells and 265 additional registers.

title: Shorten the divider feedback path to five quotient bits per clock
motivation:
The 31.991 MHz champion has a 36.909 ns Gowin path from remainder_q to
quotient_q through eight serial trial subtractions and remainder selections.
Ten CoreMark iterations took 4,491,485 marker-bracketed cycles, and the
measured loop executes no DIV or REM. This makes divider latency inexpensive
while divider feedback delay sets the clock period for every instruction.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Compute five binary restoring steps per RUN clock and register the result
after each group. Seven identical rounds cover a 35-bit dividend formed
by zero-extending the 32-bit magnitude. The three leading zero bits allow
a fixed datapath with no partial-round mux on the feedback path.

Issue, seven rounds and transfer take nine EX cycles. A load feeding a
divide adds one load-use bubble, giving a ten-cycle retirement gap with
ready buses. The prototype passed all 53 fast formal checks, including
liveness, all five cocotb suites, and cosimulation on all five test ELFs.

On the Tang Nano 20K, the prototype reached 44.763, 45.009 and 45.009 MHz
across Gowin's three placement options. The worst path moved from the
divider to the register-file read and ID/EX capture path. CoreMark with
both bus stalls passed all five CRC checks and took 4,491,485 cycles
between markers for ten iterations. The 45.009 MHz median gives 100.21
iterations/s, 40.7% above the 71.23 champion.

title: Shorten divider feedback to three radix-4 digits per clock
motivation: Gowin traces the champion's 36.909 ns worst path from remainder_q to quotient_q inside the divider. Each RUN clock chains eight dependent subtract-and-restore decisions. The champion already demonstrated that increasing divide latency costs no instruction cycles inside the CoreMark timing markers. Its median was 31.991 MHz over a 4,491,485-cycle run. At that cycle count the 4.6% acceptance margin requires just over 33.46 MHz.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the blocking divider as a clocked radix-4 engine. On issue, capture unsigned operand magnitudes and the existing sign and operation flags. In one preparation cycle, register three times the divisor. Use the registered divisor and its left shift for the other two multiples. Each RUN cycle produces six quotient bits through three successive radix-4 digit decisions. For each incoming bit pair, form T = 4R + pair and compute T-D, T-2D and T-3D in parallel. Select the highest digit with a nonnegative difference, using its difference as the new remainder. Digit zero passes T through.

Initialize a 36-bit quotient shift register with four leading zeros and the 32-bit dividend magnitude. Six identical RUN cycles consume all 36 bits and leave the quotient in the low 32 bits. Unsigned trials and multiples need 34 bits of magnitude and an explicit borrow bit on subtraction. Apply the existing quotient/remainder selection and sign correction at completion. Use the same issue, preparation, six RUN cycles and result transfer for real arithmetic and ALTOPS. This gives nine EX cycles per divide and a ten-cycle retirement gap after a dependent load on ready buses, within the configured formal liveness window.

I predict about 40 MHz median Gowin Fmax and roughly the champion's marker-to-marker cycle count, or about 89 CoreMark iterations/s. Measure both independently. The chief uncertainty is whether routing the three parallel trials per digit or a path outside the divider limits Fmax first.

title: Select EX forwarding sources one cycle earlier in decode
motivation:
The champion reaches 47.7 MHz and runs ten CoreMark iterations in
4,491,485 cycles. Its median Gowin placement shows two nearly equal
operand paths. One feeds a branch and the fetch interlock at 26.259 ns.
The other feeds the multiplier and the data-memory address at 26.246 ns.
Both pay for register-file write-through and EX forwarding before their
results can be used. Decode already has the consumer's source numbers
and the destinations of all three older potential writers.

Compute two four-way, one-hot forwarding selections during decode, one
per source. Compare raw fetch bits 19:15 and 24:20 with the destinations
currently in EX, MEM and WB. Reject x0 and qualify each match with the
producer's effective write enable. Resolve overlapping matches youngest

implementation_notes:
# Decode-stage forwarding

Median Gowin Fmax reached **57.456 MHz** across placements of 55.616, 57.456 and 57.456 MHz. Ten CoreMark iterations took **4,491,485 marker-to-marker cycles**, giving **127.92 iterations/s**, 20.5% above the 106.20 iterations/s baseline.

`core.sv` compares each raw fetch source with the EX, MEM and WB destinations. Each comparison excludes x0 and uses the producer's effective write enable, including trap suppression. The ID/EX edge captures both youngest-first one-hot selections and one shared copy of WB data. The selections and saved data hold through stalls. EX masks and combines the four sources for both operands, including store data, divider issue and RVFI. The standalone register file retains its default write-first behavior.

Two implementation choices improved placement. The register file uses the same ungated fetch fields as the forwarding comparisons, since only accepted instructions consume the reads. A Gowin distributed-RAM attribute on the register file raised median Fmax from 51.447 to 57.456 MHz with this wiring. The tradeoff was an increase from 8 to 40 LUT RAMs and a reduction from 6 to 4 block RAMs. The longest path in the median placement runs from the WB data selection through the multiplier to the data-memory address.

## Local verification

- Verilator lint passed with `-Wall`. All 86 cocotb tests passed, including overlapping writers, x0, WB/decode collisions, a consumer held behind a stalled store, and trapping JAL and load writers. The divide and load-use cycle checks passed.
- All 53 single-retire ALTOPS formal checks passed with zero failures or fix attempts.
- Selftest and three random programs matched the Python ISS both with and without memory stalls. CoreMark printed “Correct operation validated.” and matched all five canonical CRCs. Its start and stop markers occurred at cycles 15,801 and 4,507,286.
lesson: - 2026-11-22 hyp-20261122-001-r3s0 (regression, +20.45%): Registering youngest-first one-hot forwarding selects and WB data at ID/EX moved forwarding priority off both EX operand paths at no CoreMark cycle cost, and mapping the register file to Gowin distributed RAM raised median Fmax a further 6.0 MHz.

title: Predict control transfers from ready operands during fetch
motivation:
The 47.7 MHz radix-4 champion takes 4,491,485 cycles for ten marked
CoreMark iterations. IF and ID share a cycle, so every EX redirect
discards one fetch slot. The previous 128-entry direction predictor
reduced that count to 4,202,272 on two earlier cores. The regfile read
ports and the previous instruction results are already visible during
fetch. They can resolve data-dependent branch directions and common
zero-offset JALR targets before the next PC is clocked.

hypothesis.motivation:
The 47.7 MHz radix-4 champion takes 4,491,485 cycles for ten marked
CoreMark iterations. IF and ID share a cycle, so every EX redirect
discards one fetch slot. The previous 128-entry direction predictor
reduced that count to 4,202,272 on two earlier cores. The regfile read
ports and the previous instruction results are already visible during
fetch. They can resolve data-dependent branch directions and common
zero-offset JALR targets before the next PC is clocked.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use the youngest available producer to predict control flow. For each
source of the fetched instruction, start with the write-first regfile
value. Bypass a matching non-load result from EX/MEM. Mark the source
busy on a matching ID/EX writer or a matching EX/MEM load. The ID/EX
match takes priority even when EX/MEM also matches. Ignore writes to x0.

For a legal conditional branch with both sources ready, evaluate its
comparison in IF. If either is busy, predict from a 128-entry table
of two-bit counters. Form one PC-relative sum for branches and JAL.
For a legal zero-offset JALR with rs1 ready, use the ready value with
bit zero cleared. Other JALRs predict PC+4. Require every speculative
target to be word aligned and inside the 1 MiB instruction window.

Carry the chosen direction to EX. Each predicted taken target comes
from the actual instruction, and early JALR requires a current base
operand. EX therefore needs only a direction comparison for recovery.
Keep the normal forwarded EX resolution for traps, jump links, RVFI
and the recovery address. Decode raw fetch data in parallel with
resolution and squash younger work through the ID/EX controls.

A temporary prototype on the current champion completed ten iterations
in 4,151,767 bracketed cycles with both bus stalls and all five CRCs
validated. Gowin placement options 0, 1 and 2 reached 47.587, 49.383
and 49.383 MHz. The median gives 118.94 iter/s, 12.0% above 106.20.
At that cycle count the 4.6% acceptance margin requires 46.12 MHz.
The prototype passed all 53 standard formal checks and the RVFI trace
comparisons for selftest and all three random programs with and without
bus stalls.

title: Fetch the resolved target in the branch's EX cycle
motivation:
The champion spends a fetch slot on each taken transfer. IF presents
the fall-through address while EX resolves the branch or jump, then
discards the returned word. IF/ID is combinational, and EX can resolve
the successor from registered operands independently of the fetch
response. A ready instruction bus can return the target in that slot.

discards the returned word. IF/ID is combinational, and EX can resolve

aligned taken transfer this is the target. For a fall-through or a
trapping transfer it is the instruction's PC plus four. Pair the fetched
word with that same address at ID. When both stages can advance, the
target issues on the edge that moves the branch out of EX.

valid instruction in EX saves its resolved successor, including during

retried after the branch leaves EX. This keeps a second incrementer
off the path from branch resolution to the next request.

CRCs matched. Gowin placement options 0, 1 and 2 reached 63.321, 62.307
and 62.307 MHz. The median gives 150.64 iterations/s, 7.99% above
139.50. All 53 single-retire fast formal checks passed.

title: Feed decode from a two-entry fetch queue with same-cycle EX redirects
motivation:
The champion takes 4,491,485 cycles for ten CoreMark iterations. It cannot
retain a ready fetch while decode waits for data memory, a load result or
a divide. At a taken transfer, EX already knows the successor, but fetch
waits one edge to present its address. Both costs
arise at the combinational fetch-to-decode boundary.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Put a two-entry fall-through queue of (PC, instruction) pairs between the
external fetch port and decode. Use two indexed slots with one-bit read
and write pointers. Issue the oldest buffered word, or pass a ready bus
word directly to decode when empty. While decode is held, accept sequential
words until the queue fills. Allow a pop and refill on the same edge. Decode
can drain the queue on cycles when imemReady is low.

instruction address port. Its target response can enter ID/EX on that same
edge. Invalidate both sequential entries on redirect. If the target cannot
issue, remember the exact target for retry. Store the last request address
and one bit indicating whether the next sequential request adds four.
On a redirect, set that bit only if imemReady is high and older dmem work
can advance. On the sequential path, advance on an accepted bus word with
space available.
Compare load-use source fields from the sequential head or bus in parallel
with redirect resolution. A load in EX cannot also redirect. Keep both RF
reads and forwarding matches on the actual word selected for issue.
Hold speculative reads at a 4 KiB boundary until queued words drain. A
resolved target takes priority over that hold.

The champion fetches PC+4 and discards one fetch slot per taken transfer.
Its 4,491,485 marked CoreMark cycles include 294,425 conditional branches
with a nonsequential successor. Earlier bimodal branch and JAL prediction
saved 289,213 cycles. The champion now assembles both operands in decode,
so fetch can also predict data-dependent equality branches and register
jumps using values the datapath already provides.

with a nonsequential successor. Earlier bimodal branch and JAL prediction
saved 289,213 cycles. The champion now assembles both operands in decode,
so fetch can also predict data-dependent equality branches and register

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give fetch one 32-bit equality comparator. For a legal BEQ or BNE whose
sources are both ready, use the comparison of the existing MEM/WB-bypassed
ID operands. A source is ready when the instruction in ID/EX has no pending
write to that nonzero register. For ordered branches and busy-source

title: Replay the issued instruction stream through a second decode input

Decode currently consumes the live instruction bus. Even with the right
next PC, every imem wait creates an empty issue slot. The round-4 fetch
queue showed that decode can use buffered instructions during a wait,
but it depended on fetching spare words during earlier pipeline holds.
Repeated paths offer another source of instructions that can supply a
whole run of issue slots during consecutive bus waits.

title: Forward the ordinary EX/MEM result directly and interlock multiply consumers
motivation:
The champion selects among the ordinary EX/MEM result and two registered
product halves before forwarding either source operand. This puts the product
selector on dependent integer operations, branch resolution and load address
verification. CoreMark executes 93,960 multiplies in ten timed iterations,
but only a fraction have a consumer that needs the product on the next cycle.

hypothesis.motivation:

product halves before forwarding either source operand. This puts the product
selector on dependent integer operations, branch resolution and load address
verification. CoreMark executes 93,960 multiplies in ten timed iterations,
but only a fraction have a consumer that needs the product on the next cycle.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Drive the adjacent EX bypass from the registered ordinary result alone. Keep
the full product advancing beside it and select the architectural result in
MEM for writeback. If a valid multiply in EX names either source field of
the instruction in ID, reuse the load-use interlock for one cycle. ID then
captures the product from the register file's write-first port as MEM
completes. Independent multiplies can still issue on consecutive cycles.
This trades occasional dependency bubbles for a shorter path on every
ordinarily forwarded operand, including the load base and branch operands.
A multiply that consumes an adjacent ordinary ALU result still gets that
operand on time through the direct bypass.

A scratch implementation completed ten iterations in 3,167,223 marked cycles,
up 1.11% from 3,132,302. With both bus stalls enabled it produced all five
canonical CRCs and the validation message. Gowin placement options 0, 1 and
2 reached 73.720, 76.884 and 76.884 MHz. The median gives 242.75 iterations
per second, 6.00% above the champion and above the 239.53 acceptance cutoff.
Placement 0 used 4,001 logic cells, 739 registers and two DSPs. The scratch
core passed all five cocotb suites with the revised timing expectations
and matched the reference on selftest and all three random traces with
ready and stalled buses. All four ALTOPS multiply checks, single-channel
retirement uniqueness and liveness passed.

title: Select the adjacent producer's result bank separately for each EX operand
motivation:
The champion's median Gowin placement reaches 71.73 MHz. Its worst path begins
at the registered rs1 forwarding match, passes through the EX address adder
and load-hit comparison, and ends at the fetch predecessor register. The
previous round registered the ordinary result and both product halves in
parallel. Today EX first merges those banks onto one shared 32-bit bus, then
decides whether each operand needs that bus. Both decisions are already
knowable on the edge that admits the consumer to ID/EX.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move bank selection across the ID/EX boundary. For each consumer source,
compare its register number in ID with the adjacent producer's rd in EX.
On operand capture, latch three bits for that source. They indicate a match

high-half multiply writer. Qualify matches with a real nonzero destination
and suppress the link write for a jump with a misaligned target.

In EX, two 32-bit muxes run in parallel for each source. One chooses the
consumer's captured operand or the raw ordinary EX/MEM result. The other
chooses the registered low or high product. The registered multiply-match
bit selects between their outputs. This shortens the forwarding path into
the address adder, branch comparator and ALU. MEM selects the producer's
result independently using its existing bank enables.

ready and stalled buses. Of 53 fast formal checks, 52 had passed at
submission and the register-consistency check was still running.

title: Issue a dependent instruction on a predicted load hit and repair a miss in place
motivation:
On the champion's 71.73 MHz placement, the longest path runs from the
rs1 forwarding select through the effective-address adder and load-hit
comparator to the fetch predictor's predecessor register. A dependent
instruction only needs the verdict one edge later. At the champion's
3,132,302 marked cycles, a median above 75.03 MHz clears the 4.6% margin.

hit can supply data or suppress the external read.

completes the older load. On completion, patch each matching source
with the extended load result and insert one EX/MEM bubble. A trapping
load preserves the captured pre-load operands. The consumer then
executes once at its original PC. This costs one bubble on a dependent
miss and preserves back-to-back execution on a hit.

finished in the champion's 3,132,302 cycles with the canonical CRCs.

at that cycle count. The selftest and three random RVFI comparisons
passed on both zero-wait and stalled buses.

title: Start instruction replay two issues ahead to register the fetch word
motivation:
On the champion's median Gowin placement, the slowest path launches
from the successor block RAM, passes through the register file and ends
at the load-table collision check. The same RAM also feeds the fetch
branch decision. Starting its read one issue earlier gives both paths a
flip-flop output to start from. The tradeoff is that a PC two issues
back can identify the desired instruction less often at a branch.

Retime the existing 512-row instruction replay RAM. For three successive

transfer that response into a fabric register for use at C. Train row A
with C's word PC and instruction when C issues from a ready bus. Replay
requires a valid entry and an exact match to the current PC inside the
RAM window. Live bus data takes priority.

Read the block RAM every clock. If issue pauses between A and B, save
A's response on the first intervening edge and hold it until B issues.
Queue each training write for the following clock. These two port
changes remove the late issue decision from both RAM enables.

5.44 percent median clock gain outweighs the 0.51 percent cycle

title: Give fetch a dedicated operand path from the live instruction bus
motivation:
The champion scores 250.15 iterations/s. Its reported 18.321 ns path runs
from the successor block RAM through the register file to lookup_ok_q.
Fetch currently selects the live or replayed instruction before reading
rs1 and rs2 for both early branch resolution and the speculative load
table. Only architectural decode needs those operands on every issue.

When issuing a replayed word, fetch uses the existing branch counter

title: Fold RV32M execution into one registered DSP multiplier
motivation:
Round 14 exposed two expensive RV32M paths. A registered product can feed
the next EX result through the operand muxes, and the wide divider chains
two quotient-digit decisions per clock. The timed loop executes 93,960
MULs and no DIV or REM. Putting division on the same DSP used for MUL
could remove both divider feedback networks while preserving single-cycle
issue of multiplies whose operands are ready.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use one logical 33-by-33 signed multiplier with registered input operands
for all eight M operations. Gowin can map it across multiple physical DSP
blocks. On issue of a multiply instruction, load those registers from the
write-first ID operands and capture the signed extension bits and required
product half at the same edge. Interlock a MUL whose source still depends
on the adjacent EX writer until MEM can supply the value. On the next
advancing edge capture the selected product word in the ordinary EX/MEM
result register. A consumer then gets it through the same bypass as ADD.
The input registers also accept divider micro-operations during a divide.
This puts operation selection before the DSP input registers and removes
the separate product-half muxes from both consumer operands.

For DIV and REM, capture unsigned magnitudes X and D from the actual
forwarded EX operands. For D >= 2, prepare a conservative reciprocal.
Let e = max(0, floor(log2(D)) - 9), U = ceil(D / 2^e), and use a constant
ROM indexed by U to obtain M = floor(2^32 / U) >> e. Represent U = 1024
explicitly. From R = X and Q = 0, use three pairs of DSP clocks. The
first clock of each pair captures z = high32(R * M). The second computes
R = R - low32(z * D) and accumulates Q = Q + z. Zero-extend both DSP
operands for these steps. The estimate never exceeds the true quotient,
so z * D fits in 32 bits and Q * D + R always equals X.

Correct the result with parallel comparisons of the final R against D and
a 33-bit 2*D. Add 0, 1 or 2 to Q and subtract the corresponding multiple
from R. For e = 0, rounding the reciprocal down leaves R < 2D after one
pair. For e > 0, each pair takes r = R/D to less than r/512 + 2 because
the rounded-up denominator differs from D by less than D/512 and the
fixed-point reciprocal loses less than one unit. Here the initial r is
below 2^22, so three pairs leave R < 3D. Restore the RV32M sign after
correction. Handle magnitudes D = 0 and D = 1 explicitly, including
signed overflow, on the same completion schedule.

that cycle count the shared unit needs 94.432 MHz to qualify. A separate
reciprocal multiplier for small divisors alongside radix-4 hardware reached
only 83.858 MHz on placement 1, which motivates reusing the existing DSP. An
integer model checked the proposed recurrence against exact division on
441,580 boundary and random input pairs. The shared DSP design has yet
to be placed. Reciprocal setup and DSP-to-residual subtraction are its
main timing risks.

predecessor P issues. Use a 4,096-entry synchronous table of two-bit

synchronous target table indexed by P[10:2]. Its entry describes the
successor instruction Q and stores Q's in-window word PC, its direct
opcode and displacement signature, and its aligned in-window target.
Counter state can vary with history while all histories share Q's target.

At Q, compare the returned identity with the current PC and the
authoritative instruction. For a branch the signature covers every
B-immediate bit. For JAL it covers every J-immediate bit. Admit only a
legal direct transfer with a valid matching entry. Predict JAL taken
and conditional branches from the counter's high bit. A target miss
predicts fallthrough. The stored target drives the taken-PC register
directly while the match and direction drive its one-bit select.
Compute the architectural direct target independently for EX recovery
and training. Capture it and fallthrough separately so that prediction
does not select a wide recovery address before ID/EX.

Carry P's lookup keys with Q through stalls. Train direction once on an
advancing legal conditional branch, and train the target from the
decoded displacement even on a not-taken branch. Train legal JALs too.

responses. Preserve EX's single-cycle correction from forwarded operands
and the existing exact JALR path. Gate target use on the full source
match and window checks so aliases and changed live instructions recover
through the existing direction-mismatch mechanism. Measure cold target
misses separately from direction misses and score the three-placement
median. The combined target lookup has not been timed.
